title: Percentages, Ratios and Averages Under Time Pressure
objectives: Convert a percentage into a multiplier and compute p% of a number mentally using 10%-anchored shortcuts
Combine successive percentage changes by multiplying factors instead of adding percentages
Split a quantity using ratios, including ratios combined through a shared middle term
Compute weighted averages and use the consecutive-sequence average shortcut, with sanity checks
motivation: Numerical reasoning screens give roughly 60-90 seconds per question, and the difference between finishing and not finishing is method, not IQ. The candidate who computes 15% of 240 by long multiplication loses the question to the one who sees 24 + 12. This lesson builds a small arsenal of exact shortcuts - no approximations, just smaller numbers - so speed comes from structure rather than haste.

blocks.md: A percentage is nothing more than a fraction with a fixed denominator: $p\% = p/100$, so 15% is the multiplier $0.15$ and 130% is the multiplier $1.3$. Every fast technique in this lesson works by replacing one awkward multiplication with two easy ones. The single most useful anchor is **10%**: shift the decimal point one place left. From it, 5% is half of 10%, and 15% is 10% + 5%. So 15% of 240 is $24 + 12 = 36$ - no multiplication table required. The same idea gives 85% of 240 by the **complement trick**: since $100\% - 15\% = 85\%$, compute $240 - 36 = 204$. Subtracting from the whole is usually faster than computing the large percentage directly.

items: $12.5\% = \tfrac{1}{8}$ - divide by 2 three times, so 12.5% of 352 is $352/8 = 44$
$37.5\% = \tfrac{3}{8}$, $62.5\% = \tfrac{5}{8}$, $87.5\% = \tfrac{7}{8}$ - eighth-fractions appear constantly in timed tests

blocks.title: Fractions beat decimals
blocks.md: When a percentage matches a simple fraction, multiply by the fraction: 62.5% of 4,000 is $\tfrac{5}{8} \times 4000 = 2500$, computed as $4000/8 = 500$ then $\times 5$. The eighth-fractions are worth memorising because division by 8 is just three halvings.

A rise of $p\%$ multiplies by $1 + p/100$; a fall of $p\%$ multiplies by $1 - p/100$. Successive changes therefore **multiply**, and multiplication does not commute into addition. A 25% rise followed by a 25% fall gives $1.25 \times 0.75 = 0.9375$ - a net loss of 6.25%, because the fall applies to a larger base. In general a symmetric round trip loses exactly $x^2$ when the move is $x$:

blocks.caption: The round-trip loss is the square of the move size.
The round-trip multiplier $(1+x)(1-x)$: a 25% rise then 25% fall lands at 0.9375; bigger round trips lose more than proportionally.

blocks.md: Two worked checks fix the habit. First, $+20\%$ then $-10\%$: $1.2 \times 0.9 = 1.08$, a net gain of 8% - not 10%. Second, the pair that *does* cancel: $+25\%$ followed by $-20\%$ gives $1.25 \times 0.8 = 1.00$, back to the start. To find the percentage change between two numbers, use $\dfrac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{\text{old}}$: from 54 to 72 that is $\dfrac{18}{54} = \tfrac{1}{3} \approx 33.3\%$. Watch the base: the reverse move, 72 to 54, is $-\tfrac{18}{72} = -25\%$. Same gap of 18, different denominator, different answer.

A ratio $a:b$ splits a whole into $a + b$ equal **parts**. To split 240 in the ratio 3:5, divide by 8 to get 30 per part, giving 90 and 150. Combining two ratios that share a letter needs a common scale: given $A:B = 2:3$ and $B:C = 4:5$, scale the first by 4 and the second by 3 so that $B$ becomes 12 in both, giving $A:B:C = 8:12:15$. Ratios convert to fractions of the whole instantly: in $8:12:15$, the $A$ share is $\tfrac{8}{35}$ of the total.

A plain average assumes every item weighs the same. Positions do not: 60 shares bought at \$10.20 and 40 shares at \$11.10 have an average cost of $\dfrac{60 \times 10.20 + 40 \times 11.10}{100} = \dfrac{612 + 444}{100} = \$10.56$ - pulled toward the price with more weight. The quick sanity check is direction: the weighted average must sit between the two prices, closer to the heavier one. One shortcut covers a whole family of test questions: for consecutive integers (or any evenly spaced sequence), the average is simply $\dfrac{\text{first} + \text{last}}{2}$, and the sum is count times average. Hence the sum $1$ to $100$ is $100 \times 50.5 = 5050$, and the sum 21 to 40 is $20 \times 30.5 = 610$.

blocks.title: Companion practice: the Mental Math page
blocks.md: Every shortcut in this lesson appears as a timed drill on the platform's Mental Math page - percent-of-number, ratio splits and sequence sums. Five minutes of Mental Math before a practice set warms exactly these patterns; speed under test conditions comes from pattern recognition, never from rushing.

guidedExercise.prompt: A basket holds shares in the ratio tech : health : energy $= 4 : 3 : 3$, with 750 shares in total. All shares start priced at \$1.00. Tech then rises 10%, health falls 5%, and energy is unchanged. Using parts and multipliers, compute the new total value of the basket and the net percentage change.
hints: Total parts $= 4 + 3 + 3 = 10$, so each part is $750 / 10 = 75$ shares.
Value each leg with its multiplier: $\times 1.10$, $\times 0.95$, $\times 1.00$.
Compare the new total against 750 to get the net change.
guidedExercise.solution: Parts: tech $= 4 \times 75 = 300$, health $= 225$, energy $= 225$. New value $= 300 \times 1.10 + 225 \times 0.95 + 225 \times 1.00 = 330 + 213.75 + 225 = 768.75$. Net change $= \dfrac{768.75 - 750}{750} = \dfrac{18.75}{750} = \textbf{2.5\%}$. Note the structure: the ratio told you the weights, and the multipliers did the rest - no single percentage addition was ever performed.

independentExercise.prompt: An order book shows 54,000 bid shares and 72,000 ask shares. (a) By what percentage must the bid side rise to match the ask side? (b) If bids stay fixed, by what percentage must the ask side fall to match the bids? (c) In one sentence, explain why the two answers differ even though the gap is the same 18,000 shares.
hints: Percentage change is (new - old)/old - identify which quantity is the base in each part.
Part (a) base is 54,000; part (b) base is 72,000.
independentExercise.solution: (a) Rise needed $= \dfrac{72000 - 54000}{54000} = \dfrac{18000}{54000} = \tfrac{1}{3} \approx \textbf{33.3\%}$. (b) Fall needed $= \dfrac{18000}{72000} = \tfrac{1}{4} = \textbf{25\%}$. (c) The two percentages differ because each uses its own starting point as the base - the same absolute gap of 18,000 shares is a larger fraction of the smaller bid side than of the larger ask side.

commonMistakes: Adding successive percentage changes: $+25\%$ then $-25\%$ is not 0, it is a 6.25% loss, because the multipliers $1.25 \times 0.75 = 0.9375$ compound.
Using the wrong base for percentage change: from 54 to 72 is 33.3% up, but 72 to 54 is only 25% down.
Adding ratios directly: $A:B = 2:3$ with $B:C = 4:5$ gives $A:B:C = 8:12:15$ only after scaling to a common $B$; writing 2:3:5 is meaningless.
Averaging two prices without weights: 60 shares at \$10.20 and 40 at \$11.10 average \$10.56, not \$10.65.
Forgetting the complement trick and computing 85% or 95% by brute force instead of subtracting the small percentage from 100%.
realWorldApplication: Client reports, fee schedules and index weightings all speak in percentages and ratios; a desk assistant who can split a total by a ratio of 7:5 in their head or recompute a weighted average cost in seconds is materially faster in every meeting.
quantFinanceApplication: Position sizing and benchmark tracking are ratio problems: if a basket must track an index with sector weights 4:3:3, the parts method gives the share counts directly, and the weighted-average cost computed here is exactly the basis every PnL calculation needs.
summary: A percentage is a multiplier: $p\% = p/100$. Anchor on 10%, build 5% and 15% from it, and use complements (100% - p%) for the large remainder.
Successive percentage changes multiply: $+p\%$ then $-p\%$ nets to a loss of $p^2/100$ percent, and no pair of equal changes ever cancels.
Ratios are parts: divide the total by the sum of ratio terms; combine chains of ratios through their shared letter.
Averages need weights when quantities differ, and evenly spaced sequences have average (first + last)/2 with sum = count x average.
Under time pressure, prefer methods that create smaller numbers: fraction equivalents, complements, and parts.

quiz.prompt: Using the 10% + 5% shortcut, what is 15% of 480?
quiz.explanation: 10% of 480 is 48 and 5% is half of that, 24. Together $48 + 24 = 72$. (Check: $0.15 \times 480 = 72$.)

quiz.prompt: A price rises 25% and then falls 25%. The net change is:
Two funds hold capital in the ratio 3:5 and the combined capital is 240 (million). What is the smaller share?
quiz.explanation: Total parts $= 8$, so each part is $240/8 = 30$; the 3-part share is $3 \times 30 = 90$.

quiz.prompt: 60 shares were bought at \$10.20 and 40 shares at \$11.10. What is the average cost per share (in dollars)?
quiz.explanation: Weighted average $= (60 \times 10.20 + 40 \times 11.10)/100 = (612 + 444)/100 = 10.56$ - pulled toward the heavier 60-share leg.

quiz.prompt: Select every statement that is TRUE.
options: A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall returns you to the starting value
An increase from 45 to 60 is an increase of about 33.3%

quiz.prompt: Using the shortcut that an evenly spaced sequence has average (first + last)/2, what is the sum of all integers from 21 through 40?
quiz.explanation: Count $= 20$, average $= (21 + 40)/2 = 30.5$, so the sum is $20 \times 30.5 = 610$.

flashcards.back: Multiply: $(1 + p/100)(1 - q/100)$. Never add percentages; a symmetric +-p% round trip loses $p^2/100$ percent.
10% of X is X shifted one decimal left; 5% is half of that; add them. Complement trick: 85% of X = X minus 15% of X.
$(\sum w_i x_i)/(\sum w_i)$ - must lie between the smallest and largest value, closer to the heavier weights.

flashcards.front: Parts method for a ratio a:b
flashcards.back: Divide the total by a+b to get one part; the shares are a and b parts. Combine A:B with B:C by rescaling so B matches in both.
